questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that flattens what it reports
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a synthesis loses the disagreement it was meant to hold
questions.stem: Explain how a synthesis of a design review can flatten the disagreement that the review actually contained.

answer.exemplar: A synthesis is written to compress, and compression favours whatever reads smoothly, which means the qualified position is the first thing to go. Where one architect wanted a wider bay for servicing and another wanted a flush threshold for weather, a single sentence has to pick one, and the sentence that survives is the one that sounds settled rather than the one that records the trade-off. Once the two positions are averaged into a single recommendation, nobody in the room can tell which part of it their view supported, and the next review inherits a proposal that no one actually argued for.

questions.explanation: Compression favours whatever reads smoothly, so the qualified position is dropped and the trade-off becomes a single recommendation. Nobody can then tell which part their view supported.
questions.hint: Ask what a single sentence has to do with two positions.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Minutes that record agreement after a split exchange
questions.learningObjective: Explain why minutes tend to report agreement after a split exchange
questions.stem: Explain why a set of minutes tends to report agreement after a discussion in which the room was split.

answer.exemplar: Minutes are usually written to record what the project is now doing, and a project that is doing something needs a decision behind it, so the pressure to find one runs constantly against the facts. A split exchange also has no quotable form, because the useful sentence is the one both sides can repeat, and there is not one. The writer therefore reaches for the nearest shared ground, such as an agreement to investigate further, and it becomes the decision. The disagreement does not vanish, it is simply recorded somewhere else, and the file looks tidier than the room was.

questions.explanation: Minutes are written to record what the project is doing. The writer reaches for the nearest ground, and the disagreement moves out of sight while the file looks tidier than the room was.
questions.hint: Ask what sentence both sides could repeat.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A summary reporting a position no one held
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a summary comes to report a position nobody held
questions.stem: Explain how a design summary comes to report a position that nobody in the review actually held.

answer.exemplar: A summary is usually assembled from fragments rather than copied from a transcript, and the fragments arrive in the writer's memory without their owners attached. A phrase one architect used in passing about a deeper beam may sit beside another architect's comment about site speed, and when the writer joins them the result is a position that sounds like it came from somebody. The error is easy to miss because each half is genuine, so the summary reads as credible, and by the time a later reader checks it the meeting has moved on and nobody remembers arguing the other way.

questions.explanation: A summary is assembled from genuine fragments whose owners have been detached. Each half being real is what makes the error hard to catch later.
questions.hint: Ask which two genuine remarks were joined together.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A silent omission in a response memo
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a silent omission prevents the reader from knowing
questions.stem: Explain what a silent omission in a response memo prevents the reader from knowing or doing.

answer.exemplar: The reader cannot tell the difference between a question that was considered and answered elsewhere and a question that was never addressed, because the memo is silent in both cases. That difference determines what the reader does next, since one reading means follow up and the other means the answer is already on file and the item can close. Where the omission is not even named, a later reader cannot tell whether the question existed, which means it will not be raised again. The silence therefore does not merely withhold an answer, it removes the item from the list of things anyone is looking for.

questions.explanation: The reader cannot tell a question answered elsewhere from one never addressed. The silence also removes the item from the list of things anyone is looking for.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader will assume about the unanswered item.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that flattens what it reports
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to spot a flattened synthesis while it is being written
questions.stem: Explain how an architect can notice that a synthesis is flattening the review while the synthesis is still being written.

answer.exemplar: The warning sign is a sentence that has to start with a qualifier, because a qualifier usually appears where two positions have been forced into one claim, and by the time it reads as a small caveat the disagreement has already been lost. A second check is whether the sentence can be traced to one speaker, because a synthesis that nobody could have said was probably assembled rather than reported. The practical habit is to draft each sentence and then ask who in the room would have spoken it, and to set aside the ones where the answer is nobody, since those are where the flattening enters.

questions.explanation: A qualifier usually marks a point where two positions were forced into one claim. Drafting sentence by sentence and checking who would have spoken it catches the flattening as it happens.
questions.hint: Ask who in the room would have spoken that sentence.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A summary reporting a compromise nobody argued
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a summary invents compromises that nobody argued
questions.stem: Explain why a design summary sometimes reports a compromise that no participant argued for.

answer.exemplar: A compromise is easier to write than a disagreement, because a disagreement has to be reported as two things and a compromise is one thing with a plausible shape. When the writer is looking for a way to close out a section that did not close, the middle of the range is available and it sounds like the sensible outcome, so a figure appears that nobody proposed. The problem then compounds, because the invented compromise reads as the resolution and the next document will build on it as if it had been agreed. What began as tidying becomes a decision that no meeting ever made.

questions.explanation: A compromise is easier to write than a disagreement. The invented figure then becomes the resolution the next document builds on.
questions.hint: Ask why a disagreement is harder to write down than a.

questions.topic: Minutes that record agreement after a split exchange
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a split exchange can be detected in a later reading of the minutes
questions.stem: Explain how a reader can later detect that a set of minutes reported agreement after a split exchange.

answer.exemplar: The record usually leaks the split through the word it uses, because a genuine agreement is stated as a fact while an invented one is stated as an outcome, so phrases like it was agreed or the team decided tend to appear where nobody actually decided. The other tell is the record of who was thanked, since minutes thank the person whose proposal was accepted, and a split exchange usually produces thanks to nobody. A third check is to look for what the minutes do not say about the alternative, because a real decision in a room usually has the rejected option mentioned briefly and an invented one does not.

questions.explanation: A real agreement reads as a fact while an invented one reads as an outcome. Whether anyone was thanked and whether the rejected option appears at all are two further tells.
questions.hint: Ask how the entry words the outcome, and what it leaves out.

answer.exemplar: An agreement has one shape, and the record can simply state it, which is why minutes can be written quickly when the room converges. questions.learningObjective: Construct a summary that closes a section without inventing an outcome
questions.stem: A discussion section ended without agreement and the summary has to close it honestly. Which sentence does that?

options.text: The two options were discussed and the section was closed with no agreement, carrying both to the next meeting.
The section was closed with a compromise that reflects the shared priorities of the team.
options.misconception: invents a compromise to give the section an ending

options.text: The section was closed on the recommendation of the associate, which the team accepted without objection.
options.misconception: reports acceptance that silence never provided

options.text: The section was deferred, with the reasons for deferring recorded against each option.
options.misconception: reports a deferral where the real outcome was a split

questions.explanation: Reporting the two options, the absence of agreement. A compromise, a silent acceptance, and a deferral each substitute an outcome the room did not reach.
questions.hint: Ask what a closing sentence may assert about the outcome.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence for turning a discussion record into a synthesis
questions.learningObjective: Identify the risk in an otherwise reasonable synthesis sequence

stimulus.body: A team drafts its synthesis by extracting decisions from the transcript, then open points, then writing the reasons against each decision. They have found that the reasons attached to a decision sometimes read as the writer's justification rather than as what was said at the time.

questions.stem: Given this note, which risk does the described sequence carry?

options.text: The open points are extracted last and so are the first to be dropped from the synthesis.
options.misconception: describes an ordering effect.

options.text: Reasons are reconstructed after the fact from the decision rather than taken from the discussion.
The decisions are extracted from a transcript that may itself have been edited before the meeting.
options.misconception: invents a fault in the source the note does not mention

options.text: The synthesis carries no narrative, so a reader cannot follow the order of the discussion.
options.misconception: treats the absence of narrative as the risk described

questions.explanation: The reasons are added after the decisions are known. The other three risks are not present in the sequence as described.
questions.hint: Ask at which point the reasons were written down.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A response memo that engages one reading
questions.learningObjective: Select the response that engages every reading of a note
questions.stem: A client note asks whether the courtyard will be lit at night and whether the planters are included in the tender. Which response engages both readings?

options.text: Answer the lighting question in full, since the planters are a tender matter for the cost consultant.
options.misconception: passes the second question to someone else as if.

options.text: Ask which of the two questions the client considers the priority before replying.
options.misconception: asks the client to rank the questions.

options.text: Answer both questions directly, and note any part that will be confirmed in the next issue.
Answer the planter question, since the lighting detail is already covered in the previous issue.
options.misconception: answers one question and assumes the other was dealt with

questions.explanation: Both questions are answered directly, with the outstanding part named rather than dropped, so every reading is engaged. Passing one to a colleague, asking for a priority.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader must be able to find in the reply.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A silent omission in a response memo
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a memo that defers a question from one that omits it
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a memo that defers a question and a memo that omits it.

answer.exemplar: A deferral is a decision about the question, and it says so, so the reader knows the point was considered, that it needs something further, and where the answer will come from. An omission is not a decision about anything, and it says nothing, so the reader cannot tell a point that was judged premature from a point nobody reached. The practical difference is that a deferred question can be chased and a deferred answer will arrive, because the memo committed to a route, while an omitted one simply falls out of the correspondence and is likely to be asked again from scratch.

questions.explanation: A deferral is a decision that says the point was considered and names where the answer will come from. An omission says nothing, so the reader cannot distinguish a judged-early point from one nobody reached.
questions.hint: Ask which one has committed to a route for the answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Minutes that record agreement after a split exchange
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an agreed decision can also be misrecorded in minutes
questions.stem: Explain why a decision the room actually agreed can still end up misrecorded in a set of minutes.

answer.exemplar: An agreement is easier to record than it is to hold, because the record keeps only the outcome and drops the condition that came with it. If the room agreed to the detail on the understanding that the acoustic report would support it, the minutes will often record the detail and quietly lose the understanding, and the condition is the part that mattered. Where the agreement also came with a dissent that was noted rather than argued, the dissent is likewise the part that falls away, so the minutes end up claiming a unanimity that never existed even though the decision itself was real.

questions.explanation: The record keeps the outcome and drops the condition attached to it, and a noted dissent falls away too. The decision is real but the minutes claim a unanimity that was never there.
questions.hint: Ask what the room attached to the agreement that the record.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that flattens what it reports
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the effect of a flattened synthesis on a later design decision

stimulus.body: A synthesis states that the team agreed the stair balustrade would be solid oak. The transcript records an engineer asking for a steel balustrade on fire grounds, an architect preferring oak on detailing grounds, and no agreement reached. A later structural drawing was issued showing oak.

questions.stem: Given this note, which consequence is most serious?

options.text: The drawing is issued late, because the synthesis took longer to write than the review took to run.
options.misconception: invents a timing failure the note does not record

options.text: The client will object to oak, because the client was not in the review that discussed it.
options.misconception: invents a client objection and a client absence

options.text: The transcript should have been stored with the drawing so the disagreement could be checked later.
options.misconception: treats storage as the serious consequence.

options.text: The issued drawing rests on a position the team never took.

questions.explanation: The drawing relies on a preference the room never adopted. A later drawing turns a flattened synthesis into a decision that carries an unaddressed objection into the construction.
questions.hint: Ask what the issued drawing now rests on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a disagreement visible in writing
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a proposed record entry keeps a disagreement visible
questions.stem: Which entry keeps a disagreement visible in writing for a later reader?

options.text: The rainwater outlet position was contested, with the drainage engineer citing falls and the architect citing the paving setting out.
The rainwater outlet position was settled in discussion, with the reasons recorded separately.
options.misconception: reports settlement where a disagreement was recorded

options.text: The rainwater outlet position remains provisional pending a drainage calculation.
options.misconception: reports a provisional status instead of a contested point

options.text: The rainwater outlet position was noted as an item for the next coordination meeting.
options.misconception: records the item and not the disagreement behind it

questions.explanation: Naming the point as contested and giving each side its own reason keeps the disagreement legible to whoever picks it up. A settlement, a provisional status, and a coordination item each replace the split with something else.
questions.hint: Ask which entry shows two reasons rather than one outcome.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A summary reporting a position no one held
questions.learningObjective: Assess a memo that reports a position the team did not hold
questions.stem: Stage one: a memo to the client states that the practice prefers a lightweight cladding system for the warehouse elevation. Stage two: which finding most strongly shows the claim is unsafe?

options.text: The transcript shows the client asking for a lightweight system and the practice considering it.
options.misconception: treats a client request as a practice preference

options.text: The transcript shows the practice discussing three cladding systems and expressing no preference for any of them.
The memo was issued with a schedule of the cladding options considered.
options.misconception: treats a schedule as evidence about what was preferred

options.text: The warehouse elevation had already been designed with a heavier system before the meeting.
options.misconception: reads prior design work as evidence about the discussion

questions.explanation: A transcript that shows three options discussed and no preference expressed means the claim attributes a position the practice never took.
questions.hint: Ask whether anyone in the meeting expressed a preference.
